articles.title: Anthropic is making Claude ‘election-ready’ as US mid-term polls near; company says: Goal is to prevent …
articles.summary: Anthropic is preparing Claude for the US midterm elections.
articles.body: Anthropic is preparing Claude for the US midterm elections. The artificial intelligence (AI) company said it is bringing new safeguards to prevent election-related misinformation, political manipulation and attempts to interfere with voting. The measures include integrating official voting information into chatbot responses, providing updated election results, and improving systems to detect coordinated AI campaigns that try to influence voters.​Anthropic is also expanding its political-bias measures to ensure Claude responds more evenly across political viewpoints. The company said it plans to make Claude useful in political conversations while also preventing abuse that could harm the democratic process. It follows investigations that revealed attempts to use Claude to produce misleading election coverage and fake news content.​Claude to provide official voting information​Anthropic analysed about 250,000 conversations over one week to understand how people use Claude for political queries. According to the company, discussions about politics, public policy and social issues accounted for 5.75% of conversations on Claude.ai in the US, while election and voting queries represented 0.51%.​Requests asking Claude whom or what to vote for accounted for around 0.01% of conversations, while requests violating its election integrity policies appeared in approximately 0.002%.​Claude.ai will continue directing users to TurboVote, a nonpartisan voting information resource operated by Democracy Works. The chatbot will also begin providing official, state-specific information about polling locations, registration and identification requirements. Anthropic plans to share updated election results and vote counts directly in conversations on election night and in the days that follow.​Anthropic expands political bias testing​Anthropic said Claude Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5 and Haiku 5.5 scored 99% on its political evenhandedness evaluation.​The company also worked with independent organisations, including Vanderbilt University's Future of Free Speech, the Foundation for American Innovation, and the Collective Intelligence Project, to assess how Claude handles contentious political topics.​The evaluations found that Claude generally engaged with political questions but sometimes added unsolicited caveats or opposing arguments. Another assessment found that Claude Sonnet 4.5 was more likely to soften arguments supporting right-leaning positions.​Anthropic said it has improved how the chatbot presents counterarguments and responds better to direct yes-or-no questions and requests for shorter answers.​New safeguards target election manipulation​Anthropic's Usage Policy prohibits using Claude to spread false voting information, impersonate election officials or suppress voter participation. It also restricts fake social media profiles, mass-generated comments designed to inflate engagement and content falsely presented as independent journalism.​Working with the Institute for Strategic Dialogue and the McCain Institute, Anthropic tested its safeguards against election-related misuse in the US, Israel and Brazil. Researchers found that Claude generally refused direct harmful requests but could miss coordinated campaigns when individual tasks appeared harmless.​The company has since introduced additional detection systems targeting fake accounts, misleading news websites, foreign state-linked operations and cyber threats involving election infrastructure.​Anthropic identifies election-related abuse​Anthropic said foreign-based operators used Claude to produce US midterm coverage favouring Russian, Iranian and North Korean narratives through a fake news website. It also identified attempts to generate fabricated news to attract American audiences and earn advertising revenue.​The company said it banned the accounts involved and improved its detection systems. Anthropic plans to continue strengthening election safeguards and publish further analysis of how people use Claude during the election cycle.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: FBI gives update on spy device found at OpenAI's office; says: Saudi National arrested; shares 'crime photos'
articles.summary: OpenAI fired an employee after a hidden recording device was discovered inside one of its San Francisco offices.
articles.body: OpenAI fired an employee after a hidden recording device was discovered inside one of its San Francisco offices. Now, the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) has shared an official press release sharing an update on the spy device found at the ChatGPT-maker’s office. It stated that the agency had arrested Abdulrahman Alfozan, a national of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia on October 9. The 35-year-old has been charged with using an electronic, mechanical, or other device to intercept communications. As stated in the release, FBI Director Kash Patel said that “Abdulrahman Alfozan allegedly concealed a covert recording device inside his employer’s executive conference room to secretly capture sensitive communications about the company’s super intelligence technology,” saidOpenAI employees concealed spy device in toilet paperAs per the release, Abdulrahman Alfozan was employed as an engineer by OpenAI since July 2025. On or about September 30, OpenAI personnel discovered a surreptitious audio recording device inserted into a USB port on the back of a television in an executive conference room inside one of their buildings in San Francisco. The device was concealed in toilet paper and was installed on or about September 28, the company determined. The recording were encrypted, the agency said.Closed-circuit television (CCTV) footage inside OpenAI’s office showed that Alfozan appeared near the executive conference room on multiple dates prior to the device’s discovery, although he had no authority to access or to participate in meetings occurring in the executive conference room. According to the complaint, meetings in the executive conference room where the device was discovered frequently involved discussions of highly confidential technical, commercial, and strategic information, including proprietary research, product plans, and business-development opportunities, as well as nonpublic information about Open AI’s technical progress and strategic decisions, capabilities, priorities, government engagements, and commercial relationships.According to the complaint, prior to September 28, Alfozan used a productivity tool to make multiple inquiries about Open AI’s building addresses, meeting rooms, meeting-room capacities and calendars, “leadership and exec” locations, and external partner meetings. Moreover, a chatbot account associated with Alfozan’s spouse submitted prompts between September 24 and September 30 related to building, customizing, installing, audio recording, testing, obfuscating, and remote accessing a device, including inquiries about “build[ing] a continuous audio recorder,” “customiz[ing] Wi-Fi . . . connectivity,” “improv[ing] audio and live listening,” and “encrypt[ing] the SD card,” among other things.The same chatbot account also submitted prompts specifically related to Recording Device 1, including its custom header and unique MAC address, between September 27 and September 28, the agency added.OpenAI also alleges that Alfozan left a bag unattended in a different room in an OpenAI building on October 5. OpenAI security personnel found and opened Alfozan’s bag, inside which they discovered Alfozan’s wallet, ID and another recording device among other things.If convicted, Alfozan can face a maximum penalty of 5 years in prison and a $250,000 fine, followed by 3 years of supervised release.You use AI every day. articles.title: AI Race Puts $3.5 Trillion at Write-Down Risk, Gartner Warns
articles.summary: More than $3.5 trillion of AI infrastructure spending could be at risk of impairment by 2030 as the industry’s investment boom threatens to outpace the reven...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- More than $3.5 trillion of AI infrastructure spending could be at risk of impairment by 2030 as the industry's investment boom threatens to outpace the revenue required to justify it, according to an analysis by market research firm Gartner Inc.

AI data center owners would need to generate a cumulative $8.5 trillion in revenue through 2030 to cover capital spending, financing costs and achieve a 12% return on invested capital. Yet Gartner forecasts no more than $3.6 trillion in attributable enterprise and consumer AI revenue over that period — less than half the required amount.

The widening gulf between investment requirements and projected revenue raises questions over the sustainability of the AI infrastructure boom, particularly as rapidly depreciating computing assets risk becoming obsolete before generating sufficient returns.

The implications are especially stark for specialist AI infrastructure providers such as CoreWeave Inc. and Nebius Group NV. Their business models are more directly exposed to demand for computing capacity than diversified hyperscalers like Microsoft Corp, Alphabet Inc. and Amazon.com Inc.

Gartner predicts that cost pressures and limited differentiation will force more than 80% of neocloud providers to cease operating independently by 2030.

Will Sommer, senior director analyst at Gartner, said many of these neocloud providers are working to develop the higher-margin software and services of cloud providers, though few may succeed.

"All of them want to be the full-stack. They can't all be," he said. "For every dollar that's spent on compute, only a fraction of that is going to the owners of compute."
authors: Ruhell Amin, Neil Campling and Mark Bergen

articles.title: Ralph Lauren ties executive payouts to AI in sign of retail's shifting priorities
articles.summary: By Danielle Kaye NEW YORK, Oct 15 (Reuters) - Ralph Lauren, like many companies in the retail space, had until last year tied part of its executives’ compens...
articles.body:
NEW YORK, Oct 15 (Reuters) - Ralph Lauren, like many companies in the retail space, had until last year tied part of its executives' compensation to a warm-and-cuddly metric known as "citizenship and sustainability."

But in a sign of the times, the fashion label has replaced the sustainability measure with one ‌linking a portion of its top leaders' annual payout to "AI metrics."

The company's previously unreported move eliminates sustainability targets — a hallmark of the so-called ESG movement, which urged companies ‌to find performance measures tied to environmental and social well-being — from its short-term incentive plan. Those targets had been in place for four years.

Instead, AI goals were added to a series of other factors, such as sales ​growth and operational costs, as a basis to adjust annual incentive payouts for executives. Buried in a 131-page disclosure, the shift signals an emerging push in the retail sector to hold corporate leaders accountable for AI adoption.

A Ralph Lauren spokesperson said the AI target reinforced "opportunities for leveraging AI to enhance our work."

The company's prior sustainability metrics, she added, contributed to meaningful progress on its goals. "Our work in this area has matured and is now operationalized throughout our business," she said.

Ralph Lauren is among the few publicly listed retailers that have explicitly incorporated AI into incentive plans, joining companies ‌beyond the retail sector including Salesforce and Textron, which also ⁠replaced its ESG metric. A handful of consumer companies, including PepsiCo, have cited advancing an "AI agenda" this year as a factor in setting annual payouts for specific executives.

Compensation advisors say more of Ralph Lauren's peers might eventually follow suit as investors seek returns on AI spending and as consumer companies ⁠turn to the technology to boost margins.

"I'd call it an emerging practice," said Cory Morrow, a partner at Korn Ferry who leads the firm's consumer and retail practice for executive pay.

"The hard part, when you're putting something like AI in a bonus plan, is quantifying what are you really measuring," he said. "It's still relatively new at this point, so companies are just getting a baseline on anything that's ​measurable."

A ​retailer's annual incentive plan is a "messaging device" to signal what's important to the company, Morrow said, adding ​that financial metrics like sales growth and profitability will continue to ‌form the bulk of most bonus plans.

articles.title: Why not knowing may be your greatest strength: Santhosh Jayaram’s book challenges conventional ideas of intelligence and leadership
articles.summary: What if admitting “I don't know” is not a sign of weakness but the beginning of meaningful learning?
articles.body: What if admitting “I don't know” is not a sign of weakness but the beginning of meaningful learning? In a world where artificial intelligence can produce answers in seconds and professional knowledge can quickly become outdated, Santhosh Jayaram’s 'Operating from the Zone of Incompetence: Why Not-Knowing Is the New Intelligence' arrives with a timely question: how do we keep learning when what we already know is no longer enough?Published by Rupa Publications in 2026, the non-fiction book challenges the assumption that expertise alone is the key to progress. Rather than dismissing competence, Jayaram asks readers to consider what happens when they become too comfortable with their existing knowledge. The book’s central idea is that intellectual humility, curiosity and a willingness to unlearn may be essential abilities in a rapidly changing world. Drawing on the themes outlined in his announcement of the book, Jayaram positions learning as a continuous process rather than a destination. The premise is particularly relevant to professionals, leaders and anyone navigating a workplace increasingly shaped by technology and artificial intelligence.Why the comfort of expertise can become a limitationBeing good at something often brings confidence, recognition and a sense of security. But that confidence can also make it harder to question familiar methods or recognise when circumstances have changed. Jayaram’s title captures this tension. Operating from a “zone of incompetence” does not mean abandoning skills or celebrating ignorance. Instead, it suggests being willing to enter unfamiliar territory, ask questions and accept that there is more to learn.This idea challenges a common professional instinct: the pressure to appear knowledgeable at all times. In workplaces where leaders are expected to have answers and employees may fear looking inexperienced, admitting uncertainty can feel risky. Yet refusing to acknowledge knowledge gaps can make people less receptive to new ideas. The book explores what happens when expertise expires, why unlearning can be difficult and how people can continue learning even after achieving professional success. These questions give its central argument practical relevance, especially for people whose careers depend on adapting to changing technologies, expectations and ways of working.Unlearning, leadership and the age of AIOne of the book’s key themes is the importance of unlearning. Acquiring new information is only part of learning; people must sometimes question assumptions, habits and beliefs that once helped them succeed but may no longer be useful. Jayaram traces the beginning of the book to advice from Professor Deepak Gupta, who told him during the early stages of his PhD journey: “You can't learn anything new until you de-learn.” Jayaram said the conversation planted the seed for the book. The title came from a phrase used by Dr R Balasubramaniam during a talk. Jayaram asked to use it, and Balasubramaniam agreed. Both later contributed forewords to the book.The focus on unlearning also connects to the book’s questions about leadership. A leader who believes they must always be right may struggle to invite disagreement or acknowledge changing realities. By contrast, a leader who can say “I don't know. Yet” creates room for inquiry, collaboration and better-informed decisions. This is especially pertinent in the age of AI. As technology makes information easier to access and generate, the ability to ask useful questions, evaluate answers and recognise limitations becomes increasingly important. Access to information does not automatically translate into sound judgement.A reminder to remain an infinite learnerJayaram describes the book as an exploration of intellectual humility, curiosity, adaptability and becoming an “infinite learner”. Rather than telling readers what they should know, he says he wants to change how they relate to what they do not know. That distinction is the book’s most compelling promise. It shifts the focus from collecting qualifications or accumulating expertise to developing an attitude that remains open to revision. For students, this could mean treating mistakes as opportunities to improve. For professionals, it could mean questioning familiar routines. For leaders, it could mean making space for people who challenge established thinking.The idea is not entirely new: lifelong learning and intellectual humility have long been discussed in education and leadership. The strength of Jayaram’s framing lies in placing these ideas against a contemporary backdrop of rapid technological change and the growing uncertainty around which skills will remain relevant. A critical assessment of how successfully the book develops its arguments, supports them with examples and translates them into practical guidance would require examining the full text. Based on its stated themes, however, it offers a useful starting point for readers willing to question the pressure to appear competent all the time.Operating from the Zone of Incompetence ultimately invites readers to see uncertainty not as a dead end, but as an opening. Its message is simple: intelligence is not only about what we know, but also about how honestly we recognise what we have yet to learn.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient.
